::: {.cite-bar .domain-foundations}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [1 Stat. 381]{.cite} [18 U.S.C. 958-962]{.cite}
:::

Makes it a crime for private persons to wage war from U.S. territory against a country with which the United States is at peace. It was passed to keep Americans from dragging the country into the wars of the French Revolution.

## Key provisions

- 18 U.S.C. 960: organizing or funding a military expedition from the United States against a friendly foreign state.
- 18 U.S.C. 958-959: accepting a foreign commission, or enlisting others in foreign service, against a friendly state.
- 18 U.S.C. 962: arming a vessel for use against a friendly state.

## Why it matters

It establishes that the decision to use force abroad belongs to the government and not to private citizens. The [Logan Act](logan-1799.qmd) applies the same idea to diplomacy, and the [Espionage Act](espionage-1917.qmd) added to its enforcement provisions. It is distinct from the arms embargo laws of the 1930s that share its name.

## Current status

In force as recodified. Prosecutions are rare.
